title: A financial integrity framework for permissionless networks
gist: Major TradFi institutions are already tokenizing funds on public permissionless blockchains, and the author argues the widespread belief that BSA/AML and sanctions law force institutions onto permissioned networks is a misreading of existing law and recent regulator guidance (OCC, FinCEN, OFAC), not a legal requirement.

insights.claim: Franklin Templeton has maintained the official share register of its onchain U.S. government money fund on permissionless blockchains since 2021 and added the Solana network in February 2025.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Shows a large regulated asset manager has multi-year, multi-chain precedent for running official fund records on public permissionless infrastructure, undercutting the 'compliance requires permissioned networks' assumption.
insights.quote: Franklin Templeton has kept the official share register of its onchain U.S. government money fund on permissionless blockchains since 2021 and added the Solana network in February 2025.
insights.locator: Opening paragraph, Many financial institutions are taking advantage

insights.claim: BlackRock has issued shares of its tokenized money market fund on the Ethereum network since March 2024, and Apollo made tokenized access to its Diversified Credit Fund available across six permissionless networks starting January 2025.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Signals a fast-broadening cohort of top-tier asset managers treating permissionless chains as production infrastructure for regulated products, a trend the author says continues on a near-weekly basis.
insights.quote: BlackRock has issued shares of its tokenized money market fund on Ethereum since March 2024. And in January 2025, Apollo made tokenized access to its Diversified Credit Fund available across six permissionless networks.
insights.locator: Opening paragraph, following Franklin Templeton example

themes.theme: The permissioned-network premise is a legal misreading

insights.claim: Many banks, broker-dealers, and asset managers are trending toward permissioned networks because they wrongly believe a known, verified set of actors is a legal precondition for complying with the Bank Secrecy Act (AML/CFT) and U.S. sanctions laws.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: If this premise is wrong, institutions currently limiting themselves to permissioned chains are foregoing optionality (liquidity, interoperability, cost) for no actual legal benefit.
insights.quote: These institutions are currently choosing permissioned networks because they believe — wrongly — they must.
insights.locator: Second paragraph, Yet, some TradFi institutions still treat permissionless networks

insights.claim: There is no regulatory precondition requiring financial institutions to own, screen, or censor the underlying network infrastructure over which their transactions travel; institutions can satisfy AML/sanctions obligations through risk-based compliance controls placed at the layer they actually operate.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Gives compliance teams a legal basis to build controls at the application/customer layer rather than demanding control over network validators, potentially unlocking permissionless-chain deployment for regulated products.
insights.quote: There is no precondition — regulatory or otherwise — for financial institutions to own, screen, or censor the underlying infrastructure over which their financial transactions, and the communications about them, travel.
insights.locator: End of intro section, To put it simply, institutional compliance departments

insights.claim: Federal banking regulators and FinCEN require AML/CFT programs to be only 'reasonably designed' with effective processes to identify, measure, monitor and control risk — not to eliminate illicit activity entirely, and FinCEN's August 2020 Statement on Enforcement explicitly disavows a 'gotcha' enforcement approach.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Compliance teams overestimating regulatory risk tolerance may be over-engineering restrictive network choices; citing the 'reasonably designed' standard can justify permissionless deployment with proportionate controls.
insights.quote: FinCEN stated the point more plainly in its August 2020 Statement on Enforcement, describing its approach to BSA enforcement as something other than a "gotcha" game.
insights.locator: What financial integrity laws require section

insights.claim: Treasury's de-risking report found that severe BSA/AML fines are rare and historically follow the collapse of an entire compliance program, not the isolated shortcomings a risk-based approach will occasionally produce.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Reduces the perceived tail-risk cost of engaging with permissionless networks, since enforcement targets systemic program failure, not incidental exposure.
insights.quote: Treasury's report on de-risking addressed the underlying fear directly, observing that while banks believe any failure in banking controls exposes them to substantial fines, the regulators note that such fines are rare and follow the collapse of an entire AML/CFT program, rather than the limited shortcomings a risk-based approach will sometimes produce.
insights.locator: What financial integrity laws require section

insights.claim: OFAC's Framework for Compliance Commitments defines an effective sanctions program by five components — management commitment, risk assessment, internal controls, testing and auditing, and training — scaled to an institution's size, products, customers, and geography, rather than requiring elimination of all sanctions exposure.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Gives institutions a concrete, five-part checklist to justify a risk-based sanctions program for permissionless-network activity to examiners.
insights.locator: OFAC's Framework for Compliance Commitments list

themes.theme: Regulators already blessed the protocol-mediated fee analogy

insights.claim: In November 2025, the OCC's Interpretive Letter 1186 confirmed that a bank may pay network fees on blockchain networks and hold as principal the crypto-assets needed to pay them, building on Interpretive Letter 1174 (January 2021), which held that a bank may validate, store, and record payment transactions by serving as a node — and neither letter distinguishes permissioned from permissionless networks.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: This is a direct, citable regulatory precedent that banks can act as validators/fee-payers on public chains like Ethereum, removing a key legal blocker cited by compliance departments.
insights.quote: The letter uses the example of the Ethereum blockchain, a permissionless network whose protocol selects validators pseudo-randomly. None of the letters in this line distinguishes permissioned networks from permissionless ones.
insights.locator: Attenuated, protocol-mediated contact section, Regulators have confirmed this

insights.claim: Because permissionless-network protocols assign block-proposal rights and set fees pseudo-randomly and identically for every user, an institution cannot choose its validator, cannot bargain over the fee, and cannot learn the validator's identity — making this legally analogous to a phone call routed through switches or an email routed through third-party routers in a sanctioned jurisdiction, which sanctions law does not treat as a violation.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Provides a clean legal frame ('neutral, protocol-mediated carriage') that compliance and legal teams can use to argue permissionless-network participation does not itself create sanctions liability.
insights.quote: A U.S. financial institution whose internet protocol packets traverse infrastructure in a sanctioned jurisdiction is not considered to violate sanctions on that basis: The same analysis of neutral, protocol-mediated carriage applies to a permissionless network's consensus layer.

insights.claim: The Bank Secrecy Act's own regulatory definition of money transmitter expressly excludes parties that 'merely provide the delivery, communication, or network access services' used to support money transmission — directly covering validators as neutral infrastructure rather than counterparties.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: A specific statutory carve-out institutions can point to when arguing validators and node operators are not 'dealings' subject to sanctions/BSA scrutiny.
insights.quote: That distinction is codified in the BSA's own regulatory definition, which expressly excludes those who "merely provide the delivery, communication, or network access services used by a money transmitter to support money transmission services."

insights.claim: In the nearly five years since OFAC published its 2021 Sanctions Compliance Guidance for the Virtual Currency Industry, no enforcement action has been predicated on a validator proposing a block that happened to contain a sanctioned party's transaction, nor on a market participant's payment of protocol-level fees.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: A five-year track record of zero enforcement on this exact fact pattern is strong empirical evidence the feared liability is largely theoretical, weakening the risk case for avoiding permissionless chains.
insights.quote: no enforcement action has been predicated on a validator having proposed a block that happened to contain a sanctioned party's transaction, and none has rested on a market participant's payment of protocol-level fees.

themes.theme: Privacy and compliance are compatible, not opposed

insights.claim: Cryptographic techniques now let an institution prove a compliance-relevant fact — such as a counterparty being off the Specially Designated Nationals List, or reserves exceeding liabilities — without publishing the underlying data, giving a supervisor better assurance than a closed system while revealing nothing to competitors.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Reframes privacy from a blocker to an advantage for institutional adoption of public chains — worth tracking which providers commercialize proof-of-reserves/proof-of-unsanctioned-status tooling first.
insights.quote: Together, these cryptographic advances give a supervisor better assurance than a closed system provides. And it does so while giving a competitor nothing at all, which turns privacy from an objection into a reason to build on permissionless networks.
insights.locator: Privacy and compliance are compatible section

insights.claim: Privacy-preserving compliance tooling has an uneven maturity curve: address rotation, account abstraction, omnibus/tiered custody structures, and Travel Rule messaging are already in production; confidential transfers with an auditor viewing key are shipping but thinly used at institutional scale; and proofs of unsanctioned status or provenance against a designated set remain in pilot testing and research, with Privacy Cash (built on Ethereum and Solana using zero-knowledge proofs) cited as an existing example.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete adoption-readiness map: bet on address rotation/custody-structure vendors now, treat auditor-key confidential transfers as early-stage, and watch proof-of-provenance/unsanctioned-status tooling as the next unlock still in R&D.
insights.quote: Privacy Cash, for example, is a privacy protocol that sits on top of Ethereum and Solana and uses zero-knowledge proofs to enable confidential transfers and swaps.
insights.locator: Privacy and compliance are compatible section, list of techniques

themes.theme: A nine-component compliance framework, and its GENIUS Act parallel

insights.claim: The paper proposes a nine-component financial integrity framework for permissionless-network activity split across two layers: transaction-layer controls (KYC/CIP/CDD/EDD, wallet and counterparty screening, transaction monitoring, Travel Rule/Funds Transfer Rule compliance, proportionate sanctions controls) applied to customers largely as done today, and network-layer controls (third-party risk management of node/staking/analytics vendors) plus shared controls (governance, wallet/key management and cybersecurity, and testing/audit/training) — explicitly not requiring validator identification or gatekeeper membership petitions.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Offers compliance and product teams a ready-made, regulator-aligned checklist to greenlight permissionless-network deployment without redesigning their entire AML/sanctions program.
insights.quote: These controls do not require identification of validators, service-level agreements with a protocol, or petitions to a gatekeeper for membership, among other features of permissioned networks: The current financial integrity laws do not require any of this.
insights.locator: A risk-management framework for permissionless networks section

insights.claim: The proposed framework mirrors the GENIUS Act's approach, which places AML/CFT and sanctions obligations on permitted payment stablecoin issuers at the application layer (certifying AML/sanctions programs and maintaining freeze/burn capability), with those obligations running to the issuer rather than to the permissionless networks the stablecoins circulate on.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Recent binding legislation already codifies the 'controls at the application layer, not the network layer' model the author advocates, strengthening the legal case and signaling where regulatory expectations are heading for other permissionless-network products.
insights.quote: GENIUS requires permitted payment stablecoin issuers, as identifiable regulated entities at the application layer, to certify the existence of AML programs and sanctions compliance programs, and to maintain the technical capability to execute lawful orders to freeze or burn outstanding stablecoins. These obligations run to the issuer, not to the permissionless networks on which stablecoins circulate.

insights.claim: A generation ago, regulated institutions faced the same dilemma with the open, permissionless internet and resolved it by moving businesses onto open protocols while building controls at the application layer — the author argues the identical playbook applies now to permissionless blockchain networks.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Historical precedent (internet adoption) suggests institutions that build application-layer controls rather than avoiding the open network entirely will end up as the long-run winners, as happened with the internet.
insights.quote: Institutions moved their businesses onto the open protocols of the internet and built their controls at the application layer. The same can be done now for permissionless networks.

insights.claim: Dollar-denominated activity on permissionless networks is already happening and will continue regardless of whether U.S. institutions participate, and U.S. financial enforcement's reach depends on institutions actually observing and monitoring that on-chain activity.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Rettig
insights.so_what: Institutional non-participation doesn't reduce systemic risk — it removes the very monitoring capability that underpins U.S. financial enforcement, implying regulators have an incentive to keep clarifying rules (as with the OCC/GENIUS Act moves) to pull institutions in rather than keep them out.
insights.quote: And dollar-denominated activity on permissionless networks is already happening and will continue,whether or not U.S. institutions take part. The reach of U.S. financial enforcement rests on line of sight into financial flows...
insights.locator: Final paragraph, Avoiding permissionless networks is not a financial integrity strategy
